newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Kabul claims gains against Taleban rebels.
newsitem.headline: Kabul claims gains against Taleban rebels.

text.p: The Afghan govenrment said on Wednesday it had scored victories against the rebel Taleban Islamic militia around the capital Kabul and in the eastern province of Laghman.

Iran's deputy foreign minister Alaeddin Boroujerdi was also in Kabul on Wednesday and held talks with President Burhanuddin Rabbani and Prime Minister Gulbuddin Hekmatyar, the official Kabul Radio said.
No details of the talks were available.

A government spokesman said forces loyal to President Burhanuddin Rabbani had repulsed an overnight Taleban assault in the south and southeast of Kabul and taken territory in Laghman, which Taleban had seized last week after taking the adjoining Nangarhar province from a neutral ruling council.
Government forces have captured Chahr Bagh and Alikhel areas of Laghman and were besieging the provincial capital of Mehtar Lam, said the spokesman quoted by Kabul Radio.

There was no independent confirmation of this report. But a Pakistan-based private Afghan news service said fighting was raging between government and Taleban forces in Alising valley north of Mehtar Lam.
The Afghan Islamic Press also said some pro-government commanders had concentrated their fighters in northern Nangarhar's mountainous Shewa area to confront Taleban.
Earlier, a government spokesman in Kabul said at least five people were killed and 15 wounded in overnight Taleban shelling on a southern suburb of the capital.
The Tuesday night shelling on government positions was the deadliest on Kabul after last week's Taleban capture of the two eastern provinces of Nangarhar and Laghman.
The spokesman said government bombardment hit a Taleban arsenal in the southwest of the capital, from where a huge column of smoke was rising on Wednesday morning.
Those killed in the Taleban shelling included a woman, whose child was injured.
Taleban forces, which control more than half of Afghanistan, have besieged Kabul since last October in their drive to oust President Burhanuddin Rabbani's government.

Diplomats said the Taleban advances in eastern Afghanistan were a setback to the government but would not shift the balance of power decisively or end the civil war which has ripped the country apart since the fall of a communist government in April 1992.
